metadata.title: Labor Productivity vs. Real Wage Decoupling
metadata.visual_form: Animated Divergence Wedge with Floating Value Callouts
metadata.data_notes: Quarterly data, smoothed to monthly by straight-line fill between quarters.

events.label: Productivity and real pay start to separate
Internet boom lifts output per hour
COVID: low-paid jobs vanish, so average pay jumps
Inflation cuts real pay by about 5%

explanation.summary: Since 1950, how much more does a worker produce in an hour, and how much more is a worker paid for that hour after inflation? For about 25 years both grew together. Since the early 1970s, output per hour has grown much faster than real pay.
explanation.methodology: Output per hour (PRS85006093) and real hourly compensation (PRS85006153) for the nonfarm business sector from the BLS productivity program, rebased so that 1950 = 100. Compensation includes wages and benefits, adjusted for inflation. Corporate profits after tax from BEA via FRED (CP), in current dollars. Quarterly data is filled to monthly with straight lines.

key_findings.title: 1973: The Split Begins
key_findings.description: Until 1973, output per hour (177) and real pay (174) had grown almost exactly together since 1950.
key_findings.significance: After this point the two lines separate.

key_findings.title: 2000: The Gap Widens
key_findings.description: By 2000, output per hour had reached 278 while real pay was 230. The internet boom made workers more productive, but only part of that showed up in their pay.
key_findings.significance: Higher productivity does not automatically become higher pay.

key_findings.title: Today: A Wide Gap
key_findings.description: As of 2026, output per hour is 466 and real pay is 285. Since 1973, productivity rose about 163% and real pay about 64%. Corporate profits are a record $4.3 trillion a year.
key_findings.significance: Most of the extra output since 1973 has not gone to hourly pay.
